560d2bd4-d4f6-44da-bef5-278c8824a999.one_liner: A long-volatility PM argues the AI capex boom is now a credit story rolling over -- Oracle's CDS trading like junk, private credit acting like a 'slow-motion shadow bank run,' and Japan's carry trade as the likely trigger for the next leverage unwind.
560d2bd4-d4f6-44da-bef5-278c8824a999.recap: Portfolio manager Ben Bray (Deductive Capital), who runs a long-volatility strategy while also working in AI, argues markets are past the peak of the AI-driven momentum trade and rolling over, comparing the cycle to the 1840s British railway mania and the dot-com bust: the technology is real, but that doesn't protect shareholders or capital. He notes Oracle's stock fell over 60% from its post-hyperscaler-announcement high near $341, while its CDS widened from roughly 45bp to about 200bp publicly (300bp in private markets), now trading like junk credit. He frames private credit as a regulatory-arbitrage successor to pre-GFC bank underwriting, describing rising NAV redemption requests being gated quarter after quarter as a 'slow-motion shadow bank run,' and cites a claim (sourced loosely to BIS) that only ~40% of private credit loans generate positive free cash flow. He details the 'Magnetar 2.0' dynamic behind CoreWeave's financing, echoing the hedge fund's pre-GFC CDO equity-tranche trade, and flags credit default swaps newly listed on Meta, CoreWeave and SpaceX as evidence sentiment has shifted from pure volume-chasing to demand for protection. He sees Japan -- via negative real rates, energy-import pressure, and the yen carry trade funding global asset purchases including private credit -- as the probable trigger for a broader deleveraging, alongside a historical Fed pattern of tightening excessively right before cycle turns. He closes arguing the real risk is a slow multi-year unwind (like 2000-03 or 2007-09) rather than a single crash, driven by leverage ('the fuel') meeting a shrinking collateral base.
terms: CDS -- credit default swap, insurance-like contract paying out on a bond/loan default
CDX -- an index of CDS referencing a basket of investment-grade (IG) or high-yield (HY) corporate credits
BDC -- business development company, a listed vehicle that makes private/direct loans to companies
NAV -- net asset value, the per-unit value of a fund's holdings
CDO -- collateralized debt obligation, a structured product pooling debt into tranches of varying seniority

a9743af4-d3f2-4d12-9945-718bb7e22876.recap: Jeff Snider and George Gammon (recorded Aug 11) dissect the ~$500bn Nvidia/BlackRock-and-peers MOU to finance AI buildout, arguing it repackages ailing private credit as a 'new asset class' collateralized by GPUs rather than borrower cash flow — analogous to lending against a depreciating asset with no market to foreclose into. They flag that Nvidia backstopping roughly 25% of the risk signals borrowers can't clear a market rate, and liken the structure to a father (Nvidia) whose own income depends on his insolvent son's (OpenAI-type) burn rate. They connect this to a genuine shift in credit-market behavior: since early July, demand for CDS protection (even on solid names like Meta, used as broad hedges) has been rising steadily — not panic, but a clear change from blank-check lending to active hedging. They cite Michael Burry's 1987-crash warning and Norway's $2tn sovereign wealth fund stress-testing a 35% drawdown as signs sentiment is turning, though they read widespread bearishness (including lifelong bond bull Lacey Hunt flipping bearish) as a contrarian signal that a top isn't imminent. The second half is a rates framework: the 30-year hit a post-2007 high, but Gammon argues long rates simply track nominal GDP (85%+ historical correlation) and growth/inflation expectations, not deficits or auction results, and that Fed cuts can coincide with rising long yields because markets read capitulation as a signal to price recovery, not looser policy.

d0662ea4-7a05-474b-97b6-e5992abd40bf.recap: Macro investor Ed Dowd argues private credit has effectively become the new junk-bond market, but opaque, illiquid and self-marked -- riskier credits have migrated there from public high yield, leaving public HY spreads artificially tight while masking deterioration. He cites widening CCC spreads (noted by Gundlach, who called it 'garbage lending'), loans marked at par one month and near-zero the next, and rising fund redemptions with stalling inflows as evidence a credit-loss cycle (per a PIMCO note) is beginning. He traces the root to weak 'K-shaped' consumer fundamentals (First Brands, Tricolor bankruptcies), unreliable labor data (QCEW revisions showing non-farm payrolls off by 8 and 4 standard deviations in 2024-25), and private credit's 50-75% two-year asset growth funded by bank lending, which JPMorgan is reportedly now curtailing. He flags contagion channels: CLO downgrades forcing institutional sales, banks pulling credit lines, and rising demand for significant risk transfers (SRTs) as insiders quietly hedge while publicly downplaying risk -- a pattern he likens to pre-2008 CDS demand. He connects this to AI: the last credit impulse funded data-center/chip capex (Morgan Stanley estimated $1.5tn in external financing needed), semiconductors are now 19% of the S&P 500, and AI/AI-adjacent names are 40-45% of market cap, leaving equities vulnerable to a credit-driven drawdown. He also flags falling 3-month T-bill rates and a strengthening dollar (dollar shortage) as things to watch, expecting Fed cuts within six months.
terms: SRT -- significant risk transfer, a structure banks use to transfer credit risk on a loan portfolio off their balance sheet
CLO -- collateralized loan obligation, a securitization backed by a pool of leveraged loans
QCEW -- Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, a lagging but comprehensive benchmark dataset used to revise non-farm payroll estimates
CCC -- a below-investment-grade credit rating tier indicating high default risk
